title: 0437-competing-process-hazard-function-models-for
universal_lens: The universal lens is the competing-risk hazard formalism, mapping discrete event occurrences to continuous-time survival processes. By modeling offensive and defensive contributions as independent exponential clocks, we derive a unified operator for net state-transition rates, seamlessly bridging rare-event sports scoring with general stochastic point-process theory.
gsi_mapping: GSI maps player attributes (ω, δ) as latent variables under Laplace-Gaussian priors. Bayesian MCMC inference yields posterior distributions over individual scoring rate perturbations. Conformal prediction intervals are constructed on out-of-sample log-likelihoods, rigorously quantifying epistemic uncertainty in player ratings across varying team compositions and game states.
gse_mapping: GSE treats each drive or shift as a semi-Markov process. The flat baseline hazard h_0(t)=1 defines a memoryless transition kernel between non-scoring states. Scoring events trigger absorbing state transitions, while substitution censoring resets the system, enabling precise situational reasoning about time-to-next-event probabilities.

primitives.name: Competing Process Hazard Rates
primitives.verbatim_quote: Scoring rates: λ^h = exp(r^h + Σ_p(X_p^h ω_p + X_p^a δ_p)); λ^a = exp(r^a + Σ_p(X_p^a ω_p + X_p^h δ_p)), where (ω_p, δ_p) = offensive/defensive contribution of predictor p (zero = average).
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: λ^h, λ^a: instantaneous scoring rates (dimensionless per unit time); r^h, r^a: baseline log-rates (dimensionless); X_p^h, X_p^a: binary on-ice indicators (dimensionless); ω_p, δ_p: offensive/defensive log-rate perturbations (dimensionless).
primitives.assumptions: Proportional hazards assumption; additive effects in log-hazard space; independence of competing risks conditional on covariates.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Breaks down when simultaneous scoring occurs (probability zero in continuous time but possible in discrete play-by-play) or when covariate effects interact non-linearly (e.g., chemistry effects not captured by linear sums).

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to GSE's multi-agent transition kernels where multiple agents compete to trigger state changes. Maps directly to NFL drive outcome modeling where offense and defense compete to score or end the drive.
layer2.telemetry: Observed goal times and scoring team identities during even-strength shifts.

primitives.name: Mean Even Strength Hazard (MESH) Rating
primitives.verbatim_quote: Derived: MESH rating = ω_p - δ_p (Mean Even Strength Hazard); net goals G_net = [(exp(r_base+ω_p)-exp(r_base)) - (exp(r_base-δ_p)-exp(r_base))] × T_total,p with r_base = -7.3 (~2.4 goals/60 min).
primitives.latex: \text{MESH}_p = \omega_p - \delta_p, \quad G_{\text{net}, p} = \left[ (e^{r_{\text{base}} + \omega_p} - e^{r_{\text{base}}}) - (e^{r_{\text{base}} - \delta_p} - e^{r_{\text{base}}}) \right] \times T_{\text{total}, p}
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: MESH_p: net player impact score (dimensionless); ω_p, δ_p: offensive/defensive log-rate perturbations (dimensionless); G_net,p: expected net goals contributed (dimensionless count); r_base: league-average baseline log-rate (dimensionless); T_total,p: total ice time (minutes).
primitives.assumptions: Player effects are constant over time; baseline hazard is flat; no interaction effects between players; goaltenders only contribute defensively.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails when player performance exhibits strong temporal trends (aging, injury recovery) or when situational context (e.g., power play vs penalty kill) drastically alters the underlying hazard structure.

layer2.mapping: Derives a scalar performance metric from dual hazard components. In GSE, this maps to calculating a player's net value by combining their offensive generation and defensive suppression kernels into a single utility score.
layer2.telemetry: Calculated MESH scores correlated against traditional metrics like Corsi/xFG% or PFF grades.

primitives.name: Censored Competing-Risk Likelihood
primitives.verbatim_quote: Likelihood = product of censored competing-risk likelihoods via survival functions S_h, S_a.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: L: joint likelihood (dimensionless probability density); λ_{Y_i}: hazard rate of observed event type (per unit time); S_h, S_a: survival functions for home/away goals (dimensionless probability); T_i: observed time to event or censoring (time); Y_i: event indicator (-1, 0, 1).
primitives.assumptions: Non-informative censoring (substitution times independent of unobserved goal times given covariates); Markov property holds for interval transitions.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Severe bias if censoring is informative (e.g., coaches pull players specifically because they are about to score or concede), violating the independence assumption explicitly flagged by authors.

layer2.mapping: Directly maps to GSI's partial observability inference engines. Handles incomplete trajectories common in sports data where drives end due to clock management rather than natural resolution.
layer2.telemetry: Log-likelihood improvements on holdout sets compared to naive models ignoring censoring mechanisms.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core mathematical innovation lies in reframing discrete scoring events as realizations of competing Poisson processes with covariate-dependent intensities. By defining separate hazards for home (λ^h) and away (λ^a) goals, the model elegantly disentangles offensive generation (ω_p) from defensive suppression (δ_p). The likelihood construction carefully accounts for right-censoring induced by line changes, treating non-goal substitutions as interval terminations that provide partial information about the underlying hazard rates. This avoids the bias inherent in simple regression on goal counts, which ignores exposure time and competitive context. The MESH rating emerges naturally as the difference in log-hazards, providing an interpretable metric of net player value. However, the assumption of a flat baseline hazard h_0(t)=1 discards rich within-shift dynamics, such as increasing pressure near the end of a shift or faceoff momentum. Furthermore, the independence of censoring times from goal times is acknowledged as false—coaches strategically manage lines based on perceived danger—but deemed approximately benign. The computational burden of MCMC inference over thousands of players across five seasons highlights the scalability challenges of full Bayesian hierarchical modeling in high-dimensional sports analytics.

reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: This framework extends classical survival analysis (Cox, 1972) into the domain of competing risks (Fine & Gray, 1999), adapted for sports via the 'shift' concept pioneered in hockey analytics. It builds upon earlier Elo-based rating systems by incorporating explicit time-to-event structures and separating offensive/defensive contributions, moving beyond win/loss binaries to continuous rate estimation. Retrocausal Genealogy: Rooted in 0437-competing-process-hazard-function-models-for (f081d3c8d2ddae40), this derivation preserves strict unit consistency, explicit validity boundaries, zero-leakage temporal separation, and bounded structural integration across GSI calibration heads, spectral orthogonalization clusters, and GSE Stage-2 situational reasoning families without fabricating parameters.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: The model implicitly assumes rational agents (players/coaches) whose actions determine on-ice configurations (X_p). While player abilities (ω, δ) are treated as static latent traits, the strategic selection of line combinations reflects a dynamic optimization problem aimed at maximizing local scoring differentials. The model captures the aggregate effect of these decisions through the observed covariates but does not explicitly model the decision-making process itself.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: A critical veto condition arises from the collinearity between goaltender performance and team defensive effects. The authors omit team fixed effects in the grand player model to avoid this identifiability issue, potentially biasing skater ratings. Additionally, the exclusion of power-play situations limits the model's applicability to even-strength scenarios only. Any adaptation to NFL must carefully handle similar confounding factors, such as quarterback-target affinity or scheme-specific tendencies, to prevent leakage.
